authority: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), U.S. Department of Labor
caveat: No verified federal national occupation shortage list or national shortage analysis was identified in the reviewed official sources. This is the closest verified broad national occupational proxy, covering projected U.S. employment and openings across occupations; it is not evidence that listed occupations are in shortage. The figures are projections, not current vacancy counts, and may not reflect local or sector-specific conditions. The proxy has no immigration-eligibility effect. Any immigration-specific occupation designation is a separate legal/program eligibility mechanism and should not be interpreted as a general labor-market shortage list. authority: Migration Advisory Committee (MAC), published on GOV.UK
caveat: This is an official shortage analysis and set of MAC recommendations connected to the UK immigration system, not itself a comprehensive national labour-market shortage list or proof that every employer/location has a shortage. Its review covers selected RQF 3–5 occupations potentially relevant to UK Industrial Strategy priority sectors or critical infrastructure, rather than all occupations or a uniformly disaggregated UK-wide labour market; the report notes ongoing limitations in national/local occupational data. The report was published 23 July 2026 and describes recommendations for provisional 18-month access, but does not state an operative effective period here. Labour-market shortage evidence and recommended immigration eligibility are distinct: eligibility depends on government immigration rules and implementation, and inclusion does not alone establish a general shortage. The separate Skilled Worker visa Temporary Shortage List guidance is an immigration-program list, not a general shortage measure.
effective_period: Not stated. The report recommends 18-month Temporary Shortage List access for the 28 occupations it identifies; this is a recommendation, not a stated effective period for an operative list.

authority: Bundesagentur für Arbeit (BA), Statistik der Bundesagentur für Arbeit
caveat: This is the latest verified national official shortage analysis available on the access date, not an immigration eligibility list. BA's 2 September 2026 release reports 157 bottleneck occupational categories (Berufsgattungen) for 2025, down from 163 in 2024; the interactive analysis provides results at occupational-category level, subject to reliable data. The occupations below are only representative examples explicitly named in the BA release, not a complete list, and the release does not state their individual scores/status or exact classification codes. Labour-market bottleneck status measures labour-market indicators; it does not by itself confer immigration eligibility. No separate effective date is stated.
list_title: Fachkräfteengpassanalyse 2025（年度专业劳动力短缺分析）
methodology: BA annual analysis rates occupations at Berufsgattungen level nationally (and Berufsgruppen level by Länder), where data are sufficiently reliable, using six statistical bottleneck indicators: median vacancy duration, jobseeker-to-vacancy ratio, occupation-specific unemployment rate, change in foreign nationals' share of employment subject to social insurance, exits from unemployment, and change in median earnings. The unweighted average indicator score identifies an Engpassberuf at 2.0 or above; 1.5 to below 2.0 is monitored; below 1.5 is not classified as bottleneck. The interactive page reports that the assessment covers 2025 indicators/results.

authority: Jobs and Skills Australia, Australian Government
caveat: This is an Australian labour-market shortage assessment, not an immigration-eligibility list: shortage status does not itself establish visa eligibility, and immigration occupation lists serve a separate purpose. It is a 2026 point-in-time result, not a guarantee of current vacancies or a forecast. The overall total covers 1,021 assessed occupations; the OSL page provides data at national and subnational levels. The two examples below are named in Jobs and Skills Australia’s accompanying 2026 Occupation Shortage Drivers analysis as occupations with identified shortage drivers; they are representative examples, not the complete list. The report notes Jockey was excluded from 2026 scope.

methodology: Jobs and Skills Australia describes the OSL as a point-in-time assessment of occupations shortages in the Australian labour market. The 2026 Key Findings Report states that 279 of 1,021 assessed occupations (27%) were in national shortage and distinguishes four statuses: shortage, metropolitan shortage, regional shortage, and no shortage. Results are available at 4-digit ANZSCO unit-group and 6-digit ANZSCO/OSCA occupation levels. The report’s results are on an OSCA basis.

authority: New Zealand Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE)
caveat: This is a New Zealand-wide labour-demand proxy based on four online job boards, not a census of all vacancies and not a formal shortage determination. The page warns that the link between advertisements and labour demand is complex, especially for occupational and regional breakdowns; it also notes that small advertisement counts can distort comparisons. The latest release is current through the September 2026 quarter as of the source page last updated 6 November 2026. No individual occupations are returned because the verified page's headline shortage-relevant result names broad occupation groups only, without explicitly identifying individual occupations as being in shortage. Labour-market demand evidence is distinct from immigration eligibility: an occupation's appearance on any immigration pathway list would govern immigration criteria, not itself prove a general labour-market shortage.
effective_period: September 2026 quarter; data page states monthly series through September 2026
list_title: Not applicable — no verified current national occupation-shortage list or occupation-level shortage analysis identified; closest current official proxy is Jobs Online
methodology: MBIE's Jobs Online tracks an index of online job advertisements from SEEK, Trade Me Jobs, Education Gazette, and Kiwi Health Jobs, treating online advertisements as a proxy for all advertisements and vacancies. The latest quarterly release reports year-on-year changes in the All Vacancies Index and makes occupation breakdowns available. It measures changes in advertised demand, not the number of actual vacancies or whether an occupation is in shortage. The page reports online advertisements grew for 6 of 8 occupation groups in the year to September 2026; Sales and Machinery operators & drivers showed the strongest growth, while Managers had the largest annual fall.
